Bound the work of a match

Source: vignettes/articles/limits.Rmd
limits.Rmd

This guide is for code that matches patterns or strings it did not write: a pattern typed by a user, lines from a file someone uploaded. It shows how a match can take very long, how re_limits() stops it, and what the limits do not promise.

library(zuregex)

The problem

PCRE2 matches by backtracking: when one way of matching fails, it goes back and tries the next. A pattern with a repeat inside a repeat, such as ^(a+)+$, has a number of ways that doubles with each extra a, and a subject that almost matches makes PCRE2 try them all. Twenty as and a ! still get an answer. Thirty do not: the search runs into PCRE2’s own limit of ten million steps, and the call fails.

subject <- function(n) paste0(strrep("a", n), "!")
re_detect(subject(20), "^(a+)+$")
#> [1] FALSE
re_detect(subject(30), "^(a+)+$")
#> Error in `re_detect()`:
#> ! Element 1 of `x` hit the match limit: match limit exceeded. See `?re_limits`.

So a match cannot run for ever. But ten million steps is a lot of work to spend on each bad string in a long vector, and the error loses the answers for the good ones.

Set a limit for a call

Every matching function takes limits, made by re_limits(). match is the number of steps one search may take. Here it is ten thousand, a thousandth of the default. The error has the class zuregex_error_limit, so you can tell it from a pattern that does not compile, and handle it.

x <- c(subject(30), "aaa")
tryCatch(
  re_detect(x, "^(a+)+$", limits = re_limits(match = 1e4)),
  zuregex_error_limit = function(e) "too much work"
)
#> [1] "too much work"

Keep the elements that finished

One bad string should not always lose the whole vector. With on_limit = "na", an element that hits a limit is NA, the others are matched as usual, and the call gives one warning that counts the NAs. The second element here is TRUE.

re_detect(x, "^(a+)+$", limits = re_limits(match = 1e4, on_limit = "na"))
#> Warning in re_detect(x, "^(a+)+$", limits = re_limits(match = 10000, on_limit =
#> "na")): 1 element of `x` hit a match limit and is `NA`.
#> [1]   NA TRUE

The warning has the class zuregex_warning_limit.

Set a limit for the session

The option zuregex.limits applies to every call that does not pass limits itself. Printing the object shows what it holds.

old <- options(zuregex.limits = re_limits(match = 1e5, on_limit = "na"))
getOption("zuregex.limits")
#> <re_limits> match: 100,000, depth: default, heap: default, on_limit: "na"
options(old)

What the limits do not promise

  • Not linear time. A limit bounds the work for each element; it does not make the pattern cheap. For a guarantee that matching time grows only with the length of the input, use the re2 package.
  • Not a time in seconds. match counts PCRE2’s steps, which differ in cost from pattern to pattern. Choose it by trying your real patterns.
  • Not compiling. The limits bound matching. Compiling is bounded separately: a compiled pattern may take at most 16 MiB, which re_compile_size() changes.
  • depth and heap bind only the interpreter. PCRE2’s just-in-time compiler honours match and ignores the other two, so match is the limit to rely on.

See also

?re_limits describes each limit and PCRE2’s defaults. The C API has the same limits; see Link to zuregex from C.
